description: We are a team of students, developers, and problem-solvers united by a shared curiosity for space and its impact on Earth. Our team brings together skills in software development, data analysis, UI/UX design, and research.
summary:
"MARS FOR ALL: The Analog Atlas"joins terrestrial landscapes to planetary exploration through quantitative terrain science. Created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, the project evaluates three Pakistani desert regions:Kharan, Thar, and Cholistan,as potential topographic analogs for Mars’ Jezero Crater and the Moon’s Shackleton Crater Rim.

in order to compare separate datasets reliably, we had harmonized elevation rasters from NASA’s MOLA, LOLA, and SRTM missions onto a common 463 m/pixel grid. from these results, slope and surface roughness were computed using central-difference gradients and moving 3×3 windows. Across multi-scenario similarity screening, Kharan emerged as the top analog candidate, scoring 66.41% similarity to Jezero and 13.04% to Shackleton due to its mixed dune and ridge topography.

to maintain scientific transparency, we acknowledge minor numerical inconsistencies across project records. These reflect our evolving analytical stages, where metrics were computed at different times using varying approaches, particularly transitioning from initial raw DEMs to our standardized harmonized framework. Rather than hiding these differences, we document themalongside observation coverage gaps and sensor uncertainties.


presented as an interactive WebGL 3D platform, the Atlas provides reproducible planetary terrain screening, demonstrating how Earth’s landscapes can help prepare future missions for deep space frontiers.
details:
"MARS FOR ALL: The Analog Atlas" is a planetary terrain research and visualization platform investigating whether three Pakistani landscapes: Kharan, Thar and Cholistan. they share measurable topographical similarities with jezero crater on Mars and the shackleton region near the Moon's south pole. Using publicly available NASA and terrestrial geospatial datasets, our project conducts quantitative comparisons across six terrain characteristics: mean, median and 90th-percentile slope and roughness. A mathematical similarity framework and three weighting scenarios are used to examine the consistency of the results. our findings identify Kharan as the highest ranked candidate among the three Pakistani regions in comparisons with both planetary locations (jezero and shackleton)

our project aims to contribute a Pakistan centred perspective to planetary analogue research, demonstrate the scientific potential of openaccess space data and make complex geospatial analysis accessible through an interactive digital atlas. It also incorporates research integrity, measurement uncertainty, observation coverage, resolution differences and data limitations, distinguishing topographical resemblance from complete geological or environmental equivalence.

our project was developed using Python, Flask, HTML, CSS, JavaScript and CSV data files, alongside Plotly for interactive scientific visualizations. Geospatial processing involved Rasterio and other Python libraries, while APIs and publicly available data sources supported data acquisition and integration. Visual Studio Code was used as the primary coding environment, Google Antigravity as an AI-assisted development environment for implementation, debugging, code organisation and testing (issues such as mojibake were persistent reoccurences and navigation links would often be missed out by us) and ChatGPT for research planning, mathematical discussions (figuring out the logic needed and how the equations connect our relevant data to give us our findings), problem-solving, technical guidance, documentation and development assistance. PowerShell supported file management, automation and testing, while GitHub provided version control and repository hosting. GitHub Pages was used to publish the research website. No foreign styling was used (images, videos etc). all website presentation was done using code.

our project's innovation lies in joining planetary science, computational geospatial analysis and interactive visualization to investigate relatively underrepresented terrestrial regions. Rather than relying on visual resemblance alone, it applies measurable terrain characteristics, mathematical comparisons and sensitivity analysis. Development decisions prioritised scientific accuracy, reproducibility, accessibility, responsible interpretation and transparency. AI tools assisted the development process, finding specific relevant data defined by us (such as the coordinates to find our required areas in SRTM data) and refining our ideas into a more collective approach, while the research direction, analytical decisions, major code development and interpretation remained directed by us. Ultimately, MARS FOR ALL demonstrates how open space data, computational tools and accessible web technologies can support novel perspectives in planetary exploration research.
